title: Overview
body: Python · Rust · macOS / Windows / Linux Audio for Python, without ffmpeg. sound_rs plays and decodes the formats people actually have — MP3, FLAC, WAV, OGG, M4A — from a single wheel. The decoders are compiled in, so there is nothing to install besides the package itself. First sound 9 ms on a 10-minute file Memory 43 MB while streaming that file Import 1.1 ms versus 32 ms for soundfile Platforms 3 Linux, Windows, macOS pip install sound_rs import sound_rs with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("music.flac") # streams from disk, returns immediately player.seek(42.0) print(player.position, player.duration) player.wait() What it does Playback of files and NumPy arrays, blocking or through a persistent player with pause, seek, volume and position. Streaming decode : a two-hour file never sits in RAM, and the first sound arrives in milliseconds instead of after a full decode. Decoding to arrays for analysis, one file at a time or in parallel. Metadata straight from the container header, without decoding the audio. Typed : ships sound_rs.pyi and py.typed , so editors autocomplete every call. What it does not do No effects, no mixing, no recording yet, and no plugin system. If you need a DAW-style graph, this is the wrong tool; if you need to play or load audio reliably, it is the right one. The benchmark page also says where it is slower than the alternatives. Where to go next Installation — platforms, wheels, Linux audio libraries. Quickstart — the five things most code does. Command line — soundrs --help without writing Python. The player — controls, seeking, lifecycle. API reference — every function and method.
headings: What it does What it does not do Where to go next

title: Installation
body: 01 · Start Installation One command. Wheels carry the decoders, so no ffmpeg or development headers are needed. pip install sound_rs Requirements Python 3.10 or newer, CPython. Linux x86_64, Windows amd64 or macOS arm64 — the platforms below ship prebuilt wheels. NumPy only if you use play_array , load or load_many . Platform Wheel Python Linux x86_64 manylinux_2_17 3.10–3.14 Windows amd64 win_amd64 3.10–3.14 macOS arm64 macosx_11_0_arm64 3.10–3.14 Anything else — musl, ARM Linux, Intel Macs, PyPy — falls back to the source distribution, which needs a Rust toolchain ( cargo ) on the machine. From source git clone https://github.com/Neksand/sound_rs cd sound_rs pip install maturin maturin develop --release Linux audio Playback uses ALSA through cpal . Most desktops already have the runtime library; a minimal container or server needs it explicitly: sudo apt install libasound2 # Debian / Ubuntu (libasound2t64 on 24.04+) sudo dnf install alsa-lib # Fedora Decoding does not need ALSA If the library is missing, import sound_rs fails at load time, not on the first play. Install the package above, or use a build with playback disabled. Check it works import sound_rs print(sound_rs.__version__) print(sound_rs.list_devices()) # [(0, 'MacBook Pro Speakers', True), ...] print(sound_rs.get_audio_info("song.mp3")) From a terminal, soundrs --help prints the same check as a command, with the documentation link. See Command line . No sound, or an empty device list? See Troubleshooting .

title: Quickstart
body: 02 · Start Quickstart Five recipes. Each one runs as written. Play a file import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("music.mp3") play_audio blocks until the track ends and releases the GIL while it does, so other Python threads keep running. It opens the output device for that one call. Play with controls import sound_rs with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("music.flac") # returns immediately player.volume = 0.6 player.seek(30.0) # jump to 0:30 player.pause() player.resume() player.wait() # block until it ends The player keeps the stream open, so starting the next track costs milliseconds instead of reopening the device. Details in The player . Play a NumPy array import numpy as np import sound_rs rate = 44100 t = np.arange(rate * 2) / rate mono = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * t)).astype(np.float32) sound_rs.play_array(mono, rate) # 1D, mono sound_rs.play_array(np.stack([mono, mono]), rate) # 2D, (channels, frames) 2D arrays are channels first The shape is (channels, frames) , not (frames, channels) . Passing (frames, 2) silently plays the wrong thing — check the shape. Inspect a file sample_rate, channels, duration = sound_rs.get_audio_info("music.m4a") print(sample_rate, channels, duration) # 44100 2 213.4 This reads the container header — about 1 ms regardless of file length. It decodes one packet only for AAC, whose container does not record the channel count. Decode to NumPy import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.load("music.flac") # float32, (frames, channels) print(audio.shape, rate) This puts the whole file in RAM A 10-minute stereo FLAC becomes 211 MB. For playback use Player.play_file , which streams and stays under a few megabytes. Decode many files import sound_rs clips = sound_rs.load_many(["a.flac", "b.flac", "c.flac"]) # all cores, GIL released for audio, rate in clips: print(audio.shape, rate) Choose a device import sound_rs for index, name, is_default in sound_rs.list_devices(): print(("*" if is_default else " "), index, name) sound_rs.play_audio("music.mp3", device="MacBook Pro Speakers") Continue with The player .
headings: Play a file Play with controls Play a NumPy array Inspect a file Decode to NumPy Decode many files Choose a device

title: The player
body: 04 · Guides The player Player owns one output stream for its whole lifetime. Every method below acts on that stream, so starting a track never reopens the device. import sound_rs player = sound_rs.Player() # opens the default device player.play_file("first.flac") # returns immediately player.wait() player.play_file("second.mp3") # no device setup, starts at once player.stop() del player # closes the stream Use it as a context manager with sound_rs.Player() as player: closes the stream on exit, including when an exception is raised. Without it, the stream closes when the object is garbage collected, which you cannot predict. Lifecycle State What it means Leaves it idle Stream open, nothing loaded play_file , play_array playing Callback writes audio pause , stop , end of source paused Callback writes silence, position frozen resume , stop finished Source exhausted, stream still open play_* , resume (replays) Controls Call Effect play_file(path) Streams a file from disk. Returns immediately. play_array(arr, rate) Plays an in-memory array; resampled to the device once, up front. pause() Stops producing sound and freezes position . resume() Continues from the paused position, or replays from the start if finished. stop() Rewinds to zero, keeps the stream open. seek(seconds) Jumps; works while paused. wait() Blocks until the source ends (GIL released). del player Stops the decoder and closes the stream (or use with ). Seeking Seeking a streamed file is accurate to the frame. Containers can only seek to a packet boundary, so the player reads the packet's real timestamp and drops the difference. A seek to 0.5 in a 16 kHz file lands on frame 8000, not on the nearest packet start. player.play_file("track.flac") player.seek(90.5) # 1:30.5 player.wait() print(player.position) # ~ track length, not the seek offset Seeking past the end Requests beyond the track are clamped to the last frame. position keeps counting from the seek target, so duration and position stay in the same units. Volume Applied in the callback, so it changes instantly and does not touch the decoded data. Range is 0 to 4; values outside are clamped. Volume 1.0 is unity. player.volume = 0.25 # quiet player.volume = 1.0 # unity Position and duration Both are seconds, read from the audio clock, not from wall time. For files the duration comes from the container header and is available right after play_file . For arrays it is the array length divided by the sample rate. player.play_file("track.mp3") print(player.duration) # 213.4 print(player.position) # 0.0 print(player.is_playing) # True Queue enqueue lines up the next file; when the current one ends the decoder opens it and continues on the same stream. Rate and channel count may differ between tracks. with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("first.flac") player.enqueue("second.mp3") player.enqueue("third.wav") print(player.queue) # ['second.mp3', 'third.wav'] player.wait() # plays all three Pushing audio from Python For synthesis or a network stream, feed samples instead of a file. feed blocks while the buffer is full, so a fast producer cannot exhaust memory; stop unblocks a waiting call within milliseconds. import numpy as np import sound_rs player = sound_rs.Player() player.begin_feed(48000) for _ in range(100): block = (0.2 * np.sin(np.arange(4800) * 0.057)).astype(np.float32) player.feed(block) # returns when the buffer has room player.end_feed() player.wait() Feed at the device rate for clean joins Chunks are converted and resampled independently, so a non-device rate can click at chunk boundaries. Query player.sample_rate and feed that. Threading and the GIL Playback and decoding run on Rust threads, and every blocking call releases the GIL. player.wait() in the main thread does not block an asyncio loop running in another thread, and threading.Thread(target=sound_rs.play_audio, ...) works as expected. One player is one stream. Do not call methods on the same player from several threads at once; create one player per thread instead. Device selection import sound_rs print(sound_rs.list_devices()) player = sound_rs.Player(device="MacBook Pro Speakers") print(player.device, player.sample_rate, player.channels) The device is opened once, at construction. If a device disappears mid-playback, the player raises SoundRsError instead of hanging: playback stalls for two seconds without progress, then fails.

title: Streaming and memory
body: 05 · Guides Streaming and memory play_file never loads the track. A decoder thread fills a one-second ring buffer, and the audio callback drains it. Memory stays flat no matter how long the file is. How it works The decoder thread reads a packet, decodes it to float32, converts the channel count and resamples to the device rate. The result goes into a ring buffer sized for one second of device audio. The audio callback pops samples from that buffer. When it is empty, the callback writes silence and keeps the stream alive. Seeking replaces the ring buffer and repositions the decoder; the old audio that was still queued is discarded and does not count towards the new position. Because the decoder runs ahead by at most a second, the first sound arrives as soon as the first packet is decoded, not when the file ends. Numbers Ten-minute stereo FLAC, 44.1 kHz, measured with bench/run.py on an Apple M5 Pro: sound_rs soundfile + sounddevice Time to first sound 8.8 ms 492 ms Peak RSS 43 MB 255 MB The competitor number is not a flaw in those libraries: their API takes an array, so the file has to be decoded before playback can start. Streaming is a different design. play_file or load? You want Use Memory Play a file Player.play_file constant, ~1 s of audio Analyse the samples load whole file as float32 Play an array you already have play_array one copy at device format Play a file, need the samples too load, then play_array whole file A 10-minute stereo file is 211 MB in float32. That is fine for analysis and wasteful for playback. import sound_rs # streaming: memory stays flat, start is immediate with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("lecture-2h.m4a") player.wait() # analysis: everything in RAM, decoded in parallel with other files clips = sound_rs.load_many(["a.flac", "b.flac"]) Caveats duration for a streamed file comes from the header; a VBR MP3 without a frame count reports None until the decoder reaches the end. Seeking in OGG and MP4 is exact; seeking in a stream without an index (rare) may take longer because the decoder has to walk forward. Only playback streams. load and load_many always decode fully — that is their job.
headings: How it works Numbers play_file or load? Caveats

title: Formats and gapless
body: 06 · Guides Formats and gapless Five container families, every common bit depth, and gapless trimming for the lossy ones. Supported formats Format Extensions Decoder Notes WAV / AIFF .wav symphonia PCM 8/16/24/32-bit float and integer FLAC .flac symphonia 16/24-bit, any sample rate MP3 .mp3 minimp3 ~45% faster than the symphonia decoder OGG Vorbis .ogg symphonia — AAC in MP4 .m4a, .mp4 symphonia priming read from the edit list There is no extension allowlist: whatever the probe understands is accepted. A file with the wrong extension but valid contents still opens. Gapless Lossy encoders add silence at both ends — a few thousand samples that are not part of the recording. Left in, every track gains a click of silence and offsets by a millisecond or two. sound_rs trims them: MP3 and OGG declare the delay and padding in the container. AAC in MP4 records the priming in an edit list that symphonia parses but does not expose, so the library reads the elst box itself. The result matches other decoders: a 60-second AAC file decodes to 2 646 016 frames and agrees with ffmpeg to 8·10⁻⁸ across the whole file. import sound_rs, soundfile ours, _ = sound_rs.load("track.flac") theirs, _ = soundfile.read("track.flac", dtype="float32") print(ours.shape == theirs.shape, abs(ours - theirs).max()) # (True, 0.0) MP3 is offset by 47 samples Against libsndfile and ffmpeg, MP3 output starts 47 samples (~1 ms) earlier, because decoders trim the encoder delay differently. Lengths match exactly and sample values agree to 1.6·10⁻⁵ once aligned. It is inaudible; it matters if you compare PCM sample-by-sample across libraries. Bit depth Everything is converted to float32 on decode. 24-bit files keep their resolution; there is no silent truncation to 16-bit anywhere in the path. On output the device decides the sample format — f32, f64, i16, i32, u8 or u16 — and conversion happens in the callback. When a file will not open All failures raise sound_rs.SoundRsError , a RuntimeError subclass. import sound_rs try: sound_rs.play_audio("broken.mp3") except sound_rs.SoundRsError as error: print(error) # Unsupported or corrupt audio file 'broken.mp3': ... Decoding stops at the first corrupt packet rather than returning truncated audio, except for a file that ends early: a truncated tail is played up to the last good packet. Checking without decoding import sound_rs sound_rs.is_supported_format("maybe.mp3") # True / False, header only sound_rs.get_audio_info("maybe.mp3") # (rate, channels, seconds) Neither call decodes the audio, so both stay around a millisecond on a two-hour file.

title: NumPy and arrays
body: 07 · Guides NumPy and arrays Two directions: arrays in for playback, arrays out for analysis. Both use float32 samples in the range −1.0 to 1.0. Shapes Call Shape Meaning play_array(mono, rate) (frames,) 1D, one channel play_array(stereo, rate) (2, frames) 2D, channel first load(path) (frames, channels) 2D, frames first The two directions have opposite layouts play_array takes (channels, frames) because that is how a matrix of channels is usually built; load returns (frames, channels) so audio[i] is one frame and audio[:, 0] is the left channel. Round-tripping needs a transpose: sound_rs.play_array(audio.T, rate) . Playing arrays import numpy as np import sound_rs rate = 48000 seconds = 3 t = np.arange(rate * seconds) / rate left = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 220 * t)).astype(np.float32) right = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 330 * t)).astype(np.float32) sound_rs.play_array(np.stack([left, right]), rate) The array is converted to the device layout once, before playback starts: channel folding, then one FFT resample if the rates differ. Playing a 48 kHz array on a 44.1 kHz device costs a few milliseconds and sounds correct — a naive nearest-neighbour resampler would alias. Decoding to arrays import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.load("track.mp3") print(audio.shape, audio.dtype, rate) # (9437184, 2) float32 44100 print(audio[:, 0].max()) # peak of the left channel load returns the whole file. Ten minutes of stereo float32 is 211 MB, so for long files prefer streaming playback or decode one channel at a time from your own pipeline. Batch decoding import glob import sound_rs paths = sorted(glob.glob("dataset/*.flac")) clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths) # uses every core print(len(clips), clips[0][0].shape) Threads load_many(paths, threads=2) limits the pool. The default is one worker per core. Ordering matches the input list, and the first failing file raises. Pitfalls float64 arrays are rejected. NumPy's np.sin returns float64; cast with .astype(np.float32) or use dtype=np.float32 . Integer arrays are rejected. Convert to float32 and scale to −1…1 yourself; the library will not guess whether your int16 is scaled. Non-contiguous arrays are copied. A slice like audio[::2] still works, but you pay for the copy. play_array copies the data. The stream callback needs an owned buffer; that is one copy of the track, not two.
headings: Shapes Playing arrays Decoding to arrays Batch decoding Pitfalls

title: Coming from another library
body: 08 · Guides Coming from another library Most Python audio code is three lines. Here is what those three lines become. From sounddevice # before import sounddevice as sd import soundfile as sf data, rate = sf.read("track.flac") sd.play(data, rate) sd.wait() # after import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("track.flac") You lose the array, which you did not need for playback, and gain no ffmpeg and no per-call device setup. If you do need the samples, sound_rs.load returns them in the same shape as sf.read . For a persistent stream with pause and seek, sounddevice needs an OutputStream plus a callback queue; sound_rs.Player is that in one object. From soundfile # before import soundfile as sf data, rate = sf.read("track.m4a", dtype="float32") # after import sound_rs data, rate = sound_rs.load("track.m4a") AAC and M4A libsndfile cannot read MP4/AAC. That is the case where this swap is not optional. From pydub # before — needs an ffmpeg binary on PATH from pydub import AudioSegment from pydub.playback import play segment = AudioSegment.from_file("track.mp3") play(segment) # after import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("track.mp3") No subprocess, no temporary WAV, no ffmpeg install step for your users. The trade: pydub also does cutting, concatenation and format conversion, which sound_rs does not. From playsound / simpleaudio # before — one shot, no controls, format support varies by platform from playsound import playsound playsound("track.mp3") # after import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("track.mp3") Same one-line call, but the format support is the same on every platform and the call releases the GIL. What you gain, what you give up sound_rs soundfile + sounddevice pydub Formats WAV, FLAC, MP3, OGG, M4A WAV, FLAC, MP3; no AAC anything ffmpeg reads External tools none none ffmpeg binary Playback without loading yes no no Editing (cut, mix, convert) no no yes Platforms 3, wheels many any with ffmpeg
headings: From sounddevice From soundfile From pydub From playsound / simpleaudio What you gain, what you give up

title: API reference
body: 09 · Reference API reference Nine functions, one class. Everything raises sound_rs.SoundRsError , a subclass of RuntimeError , on failure. Module sound_rs.__version__ — the installed version as a string, for example "0.2.1" . class sound_rs.SoundRsError(RuntimeError) — the only exception type the library raises. Catch it instead of the individual causes. play_audio sound_rs.play_audio(file_path: str, device: str | None = None) -> None Plays a file and blocks until it ends. Releases the GIL, so other threads keep running. Opens the output device for this call, which costs about 0.1–0.2 s before the first sound — use Player for repeated playback. file_path — any container the probe accepts. device — exact device name from list_devices() ; the default device when omitted. Raises SoundRsError for an unreadable file, a missing device, or a device that disconnects mid-playback. import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("music.flac") sound_rs.play_audio("music.flac", device="MacBook Pro Speakers") is_supported_format sound_rs.is_supported_format(file_path: str) -> bool Probes the container header. Does not decode, does not check that the audio data is intact, and does not raise for a missing file — it returns False . About 1 ms on any file size. get_audio_info sound_rs.get_audio_info(file_path: str) -> tuple[int, int, float] Returns (sample_rate, channels, duration_seconds) . Reads the header, so the cost does not depend on file length. For AAC the container has no channel layout, so one packet is decoded to learn it (~0.15 ms). Duration is None in the Python sense only when the header has no frame count; in that case the file is decoded to measure it. load sound_rs.load(file_path: str) -> tuple[numpy.ndarray, int] Decodes the whole file to float32 with shape (frames, channels) , and returns it with the sample rate. Requires NumPy. Peak memory is the decoded audio: 10 minutes of stereo is 211 MB. Raises SoundRsError for an unreadable file or when the build has no NumPy support. load_many sound_rs.load_many(paths: Sequence[str], threads: int | None = None) -> list[tuple[numpy.ndarray, int]] Decodes in parallel with a Rayon pool, releasing the GIL. Order matches paths . threads=None uses one worker per core. The first file that fails raises, and the rest of the batch is abandoned. clips = sound_rs.load_many(["a.flac", "b.flac"], threads=2) play_array sound_rs.play_array(array: numpy.ndarray, sample_rate: int) -> None Plays a float32 array: (frames,) for mono or (channels, frames) for multichannel. Converts to the device layout and resamples if the rate differs, then blocks until playback ends. Raises TypeError for anything that is not a 1D or 2D float32 ndarray, and SoundRsError for a device failure. play_sine_wave sound_rs.play_sine_wave(frequency: float, duration: float, sample_rate: int) -> None Generates a mono sine tone at half scale and plays it. Useful for checking that audio output works at all. sound_rs.play_sine_wave(440.0, 1.0, 44100) cli sound_rs.cli() -> int Entry point for the soundrs console script; reads sys.argv and returns an exit code. You do not call it from Python — see Command line . load_bytes sound_rs.load_bytes(data: bytes) -> tuple[numpy.ndarray, int] Decodes audio that is already in memory. Same shape and rate as load . MP4 priming cannot be read without a path, so AAC decoded this way may start a few milliseconds early. Corrupt data raises SoundRsError with code="format" . list_devices sound_rs.list_devices() -> list[tuple[int, str, bool]] Output devices as (index, name, is_default) . The index is only for display — pass the name to play_audio or Player . Recorder sound_rs.Recorder(device: str | None = None) Opens an input device. Raises SoundRsError with code="device" when there is no microphone or the OS denies access. Member Returns Notes start() None Starts capturing stop() (ndarray, rate) Stops and returns what was captured record(seconds) (ndarray, rate) start + wait + stop device / sample_rate / channels str / int / int Device properties list_input_devices sound_rs.list_input_devices() -> list[tuple[int, str, bool]] Input devices as (index, name, is_default) . The name is what Recorder(device=...) accepts. Player sound_rs.Player(device: str | None = None) Opens one output stream and keeps it open. Device name matching is exact; the default device is used when omitted. The stream closes when the object is deleted or when the with block exits. Methods Signature Returns Notes play_file(path) None Streams from disk, returns immediately play_array(array, rate) None 1D or 2D float32 pause() None Position freezes resume() None Continues, or replays if finished stop() None Rewinds to zero seek(seconds) None Frame-accurate, clamped to the track wait() None Blocks until the source ends; GIL released enqueue(path) None Plays after the current track; up to 128 entries clear_queue() None Drops everything queued begin_feed(rate) None Switches to samples pushed from Python feed(array) None Blocks while the ring is full; call from one thread end_feed() None No more samples; finishes when the ring drains Properties Name Type Notes device str Name the player opened sample_rate int Device rate channels int Device channel count volume float Read/write, clamped to 0…4 position float Seconds played duration float | None Seconds; None until known is_playing bool False when paused, stopped or finished queue list[str] Paths waiting behind the current track underruns int Callbacks that starved after audio started; healthy streams stay at 0 latency float | None Last device latency in milliseconds import sound_rs with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("track.flac") while player.position < 10: pass # do work while it plays player.seek(120.0) player.wait() Exceptions Raised by When SoundRsError Unreadable file, no output device, device disconnected, stalled stream, no NumPy support TypeError An array that is not a 1D/2D float32 ndarray SoundRsError subclasses RuntimeError , so existing except RuntimeError handlers keep working.
headings: Module play_audio is_supported_format get_audio_info load load_many play_array play_sine_wave cli load_bytes list_devices Recorder list_input_devices Player Exceptions

title: Benchmarks
body: 10 · Reference Benchmarks Numbers with the method next to them, including the rows where the library is slower. Method Every measurement runs in a separate process : peak RSS is process-wide, so timing and memory cannot share one. Median and p95 over repeated runs; the corpus is generated by the harness so it is reproducible. Correctness is checked in the same run: decoded PCM is compared with libsndfile. Hardware: Apple M5 Pro, macOS 26.6.2, Python 3.14.7, release build with lto = "fat" and opt-level = 3 . Scoreboard Axis sound_rs Competitor Ratio Import, cold process 1.1 ms 31.8 ms (soundfile) 29× Metadata, 60 s file 1.2 ms 31.7 ms 26× Decode WAV 131 ms 155 ms 1.2× Decode FLAC 265 ms 465 ms 1.8× Decode MP3 247 ms 272 ms 1.1× Decode AAC 361 ms not supported — Time to first sound, 10 min 8.8 ms 492 ms 56× Peak RSS, 10 min file 43 MB 255 MB 6× Playback overhead, 3 s tone 32 ms 148 ms 4.6× Batch decode, 2 FLAC files 272 ms 448 ms 1.6× Decode detail 60 seconds of stereo 44.1 kHz, median and p95 over seven runs. Format sound_rs libsndfile PCM check WAV 16-bit 131 / 160 ms 155 ms identical FLAC 265 / 267 ms 465 ms identical MP3 247 / 249 ms 272 ms 1.6·10⁻⁵, 47 samples offset M4A (AAC) 361 / 365 ms unsupported 8·10⁻⁸ vs ffmpeg Playback and memory First sound Peak RSS Overhead sound_rs Player, 10 min stream 8.8 ms 43 MB +32 ms soundfile + sounddevice 492 ms 255 MB +148 ms The playback overhead row is a 3-second tone: wall clock minus the track duration. The player number uses a stream that is already open; the one-shot play_array pays the device setup and lands around +180 ms. Reproduce it python bench/run.py # sound_rs only python bench/run.py --compare # + soundfile / sounddevice python bench/run.py --reps 9 The harness generates its corpus (3 s and 10 min, WAV plus MP3/FLAC/M4A when ffmpeg is available), runs each measurement in a subprocess, and prints median, p95 and peak RSS. A full run takes about three minutes on the machine above. Where it loses MP3 alignment : 47 samples (~1 ms) earlier than libsndfile and ffmpeg. Length is exact; values match after alignment. WAV decode : a memcpy race with libsndfile, 1.2× is all there is. AAC decode is slower than the other formats — a newer decoder with less tuning — though libsndfile cannot decode it at all. Very small files : for a 3-second tone the fixed device setup dominates everything, and all libraries land within a few tens of milliseconds of each other.

title: Troubleshooting
body: 11 · Reference Troubleshooting What to check when there is no sound, no device, or a call that blocks longer than expected. No sound sound_rs.list_devices() — if the list is empty, the OS sees no output device. sound_rs.play_sine_wave(440.0, 1.0, 44100) — if this is silent, the problem is the device, not the file. Check the system volume and the default output device; the player follows the OS default. On macOS, the terminal or IDE may need microphone/audio permission for output routing in some sandboxed setups. The device is busy SoundRsError: Cannot open output stream usually means another application holds the device in exclusive mode — a DAW, a call, or another Python process with an open player. Close one player before opening another, or use a different device: import sound_rs print(sound_rs.list_devices()) sound_rs.play_audio("track.mp3", device="Built-in Audio Analog Stereo") Linux: ALSA and PipeWire Playback goes through ALSA. On PipeWire systems install pipewire-alsa ; on PulseAudio systems install pulseaudio-alsa , so ALSA has a bridge to the sound server. In a container there is no sound server and no device: that is expected. Use load for decoding — it needs no audio device. Why the first play is slow play_audio and play_array open the output device on every call: roughly 0.1–0.2 s before the first sample. Player opens it once, which brings the overhead down to about 30 ms. with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("a.flac"); player.wait() player.play_file("b.flac"); player.wait() # no device setup The call blocks forever It should not. Playback without progress for two seconds raises SoundRsError: Playback stalled instead of hanging. If you see it, the device probably disappeared — reopen the player and retry. If you need playback in the background, use a thread or Player.play_file , which already returns immediately. Jupyter and notebooks Blocking calls work, but a long track freezes the cell. Use the player: player = sound_rs.Player() player.play_file("lecture.mp3") # the cell returns; more code runs while it plays player.position asyncio play_audio and wait release the GIL but they are still blocking calls. Off-load them: import asyncio import sound_rs await asyncio.to_thread(sound_rs.play_audio, "track.flac") MP3 samples do not line up with another library Different decoders trim the encoder delay slightly differently. sound_rs starts 47 samples (~1 ms) earlier than libsndfile and ffmpeg on LAME files; lengths match exactly. If you compare waveforms, align first. See Formats and gapless . "Input must be a 1D or 2D numpy array of float32" NumPy's maths returns float64 by default: samples = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * np.arange(48000) / 48000)) samples = samples.astype(np.float32) # required sound_rs.play_array(samples, 48000) Intel Macs and ARM Linux Only macOS arm64, Windows amd64 and Linux x86_64 have wheels. Elsewhere pip builds from source, which needs Rust. pip install sound_rs --no-binary sound_rs forces that path if a stale wheel is being picked up.

title: Command line
body: 03 · Start Command line Installing the package also installs soundrs . It exists so that a minute after pip install you can check that audio works and find the docs, without writing Python. soundrs --help sound_rs — audio for Python Usage soundrs <command> [options] soundrs play <file> [--device <name>] [--volume <0-4>] soundrs info <file> soundrs devices soundrs docs soundrs --version soundrs --help Commands play Play a file and wait until it ends. --device <name> output device, see `soundrs devices` --volume <number> 0 to 4, default 1 info Sample rate, channels and duration, read from the header only. devices Output devices, one per line. docs Print the documentation link. Links Documentation https://neksand.github.io/sound_rs/ Source https://github.com/Neksand/sound_rs Commands Command What it does soundrs play FILE Plays a file and waits. --device picks an output device, --volume takes 0…4. soundrs info FILE Sample rate, channel count and duration from the container header — no decoding. soundrs devices Output devices, the default marked with * . soundrs docs Prints the documentation URL, for scripts and open $(soundrs docs) . soundrs --version Version on one line, safe to parse. sound-rs is installed as an alias of the same command. Examples # does audio work at all? soundrs play ~/Music/test.flac # which device names can I pass to Player(device=...)? soundrs devices # what is this file before writing any code? soundrs info podcast.m4a $ soundrs info podcast.m4a file podcast.m4a sample rate 44100 Hz channels 2 duration 42:13.6 (2533.612 s) Exit codes 0 success, 1 runtime failure (unreadable file, no device), 2 bad usage. Errors go to stderr, so the commands compose in shell pipelines. Checking an install After pip install sound_rs : soundrs --version # soundrs 0.2.2 soundrs devices # a device list means the audio backend loaded soundrs play test.wav # actual output If any of these fail with an import or library error, the audio backend did not load — see Troubleshooting . Decoding and soundrs info do not need an output device at all.

title: Datasets and ML
body: 08 · Guides Datasets and ML Most dataset code wants the same thing: 16 kHz, mono, one array per file, as fast as the machine allows. That is one call. One call import glob import sound_rs paths = sorted(glob.glob("dataset/**/*.flac", recursive=True)) clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths, sample_rate=16000, mono=True) for audio, rate in clips[:3]: print(audio.shape, rate) # (frames, 1), 16000 load_many decodes in parallel with the GIL released. On two FLAC files the harness measures 168 ms against 301 ms for a soundfile loop; the gap grows with file count until the cores are saturated. One file, converted import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.load( "clip.m4a", sample_rate=16000, # resampled with an anti-aliasing filter mono=True, # channels averaged ) assert audio.dtype == "float32" and audio.ndim == 2 The order is fixed: fold channels first, then resample. Resampling before folding would do the same work twice on stereo. A window, not the whole file # first 10 seconds at 16 kHz, without decoding the rest audio, rate = sound_rs.load("lecture.m4a", duration=10.0, sample_rate=16000) # 30 s starting at 5 minutes audio, rate = sound_rs.load("lecture.m4a", offset=300.0, duration=30.0) Windows come from the streaming reader offset uses the same frame-accurate seek as the player, so the window starts on the requested sample, and the rest of the file is never decoded. Memory Task Peak RAM Decode 10 min stereo to float32 211 MB of audio Decode the same file as 16 kHz mono 38 MB Stream the same file for playback 43 MB, independent of length Resampling to 16 kHz mono is not just faster downstream — it is 5× less memory than keeping 44.1 kHz stereo. Choosing the thread count clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths, threads=4) # explicit clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths) # one worker per core Decoding is CPU-bound, so the ceiling is the core count. Feeding more threads than cores does not help; the benchmark's scaling scenario measures 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers. When not to use this Training on the fly — decode once and store the arrays; repeated decoding of the same file is wasted CPU. Huge corpora — load_many returns everything at once. For a corpus larger than RAM, call load per file inside your own batching. Augmentation and feature extraction — not implemented. This library gets you clean float32 audio; the DSP belongs to your framework.

title: Recording
body: 09 · Guides Recording The mirror of playback: one input stream, float32 samples, and the same error contract. import sound_rs print(sound_rs.list_input_devices()) # [(0, 'MacBook Pro Microphone', True)] with sound_rs.Recorder() as recorder: audio, rate = recorder.record(5.0) # five seconds print(audio.shape, rate) # (240000, 1) 48000 Devices list_input_devices() returns (index, name, is_default) . Pass the name to the constructor: recorder = sound_rs.Recorder(device="MacBook Pro Microphone") print(recorder.device, recorder.sample_rate, recorder.channels) The rate and channel count are whatever the device reports; the library does not resample on input. If you need 16 kHz mono, ask for it after the fact: import sound_rs mono = audio.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) # or use numpy's resampler of choice start and stop record(seconds) is the convenient form. For an open-ended take, use start() and stop() : recorder = sound_rs.Recorder() recorder.start() input("press enter to stop") audio, rate = recorder.stop() Writing a WAV The arrays are plain float32, so the standard library writes them: import wave import numpy as np import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.Recorder().record(3.0) pcm = (np.clip(audio, -1.0, 1.0) * 32767).astype("<i2") with wave.open("take.wav", "w") as handle: handle.setnchannels(audio.shape[1]) handle.setsampwidth(2) handle.setframerate(rate) handle.writeframes(pcm.tobytes()) Microphone permission macOS and Windows ask for microphone access the first time. A denied permission raises SoundRsError with code == 'device' ; there is no silent fallback. Limits Captured samples are held in memory: the buffer caps at 230 M samples (~40 minutes of 48 kHz stereo). Past that the recorder raises instead of exhausting RAM. No resampling, mixing or effects on input — capture is raw device audio. Duplex (playing while recording) works because they are separate streams, but they are independent objects with independent device handles.
headings: Devices start and stop Writing a WAV Limits

title: Guarantees
body: 11 · Reference Guarantees A library is trustworthy when its promises are written down and tested. This is the list, and the ones that are deliberately not on it. Errors Every failure is sound_rs.SoundRsError (a RuntimeError ) with a stable .code : Code Meaning io The file could not be opened or read. format The container or codec was not understood, or no audio was decodable. device No output/input device, or the device refused to open. stalled Playback made no progress for two seconds; the device probably disappeared. unsupported The build lacks a feature (NumPy) or hit a documented limit. usage The call order was wrong, for example feed() before begin_feed() . Codes are part of the API: renaming one is a breaking change. No panics on bad input Corrupt files return an error, they do not abort the interpreter. This is enforced in cargo test by mutating every committed fixture ~200 times per file (bit flips, truncation, appended noise) and by feeding random bytes; every case must return Ok with finite samples or a non-empty error. Threads and the GIL Decoding, playback, recording and wait() release the GIL. One Player is one stream: call its methods from one thread at a time. Different players can be used from different threads, each with its own device handle. Determinism Decoding is deterministic: the same file produces the same float32 samples on every run and every platform. tests/decode_regression.py pins a SHA-256 of the PCM for five fixtures; a decoder change that moves a single sample fails CI. Memory Streaming playback uses a one-second ring buffer: memory does not grow with file length (43 MB peak on a 10-minute file, measured). load allocates the decoded audio once; load_many allocates all results at once, so size your batches. The recorder caps its buffer at 230 M samples instead of growing without bound. A 100-cycle playback soak grows RSS by less than 20 MB (measured: 0.0 MB). Audio quality Resampling uses rubato's FFT resampler: a 20 kHz tone downsampled to 24 kHz is filtered below 10% of its level instead of folding back as an alias. Gapless: encoder delay and padding are trimmed for MP3, OGG and AAC/MP4. WAV and FLAC decode to PCM identical to libsndfile; MP3 matches to 1.6·10⁻⁵ with a 47-sample offset; AAC matches ffmpeg to 8·10⁻⁸. What is not promised A latency figure. Latency depends on the OS, the device and its buffer; Player.latency reports what the backend measured, nothing more. Zero underruns everywhere. Player.underruns counts them; on a loaded machine or a Bluetooth sink they will appear. Real-time safety of the Python API. Calling feed() from Python is fine, but Python's scheduler is not a real-time scheduler. Bit-identical output across decoders. Different MP3 decoders trim delay differently; we match length exactly and samples to 1.6·10⁻⁵.
headings: Errors No panics on bad input Threads and the GIL Determinism Memory Audio quality What is not promised
